engagement_title: Cordwain Overland spring merch drop: recover three lost graphics from flat exports and photographed samples, separate them into plates a printer can burn, and take the drop to the printer and the store page
vertical: Apparel and outdoor gear: a mid tier overland and hiking apparel label with a small direct to consumer store (Bend, Oregon)
real_brief_anchor: Primary anchor, VERBATIM from a real Upwork post: "recreate and refine several existing t-shirt concepts into professional, production-ready vector artwork for screen printing"; "We already have concept artwork and direction established"; "Recreate existing shirt concepts as clean vector artwork"; "Create front chest and full-back designs"; "Prepare artwork for screen printing"; "Follow provided brand guidelines and color standards"; "Convert all fonts to outlines"; "No gradients, halftones". Co-anchor, adapted from a second real Upwork brief in which a team had mocked up its graphics with a general purpose image tool and needed the messy raster art refined into production formats "for screen printing, social media, creating my own print graphics, etc.", delivered "both vector based with separate layers and rasterized" with "spot color info", in a muted palette. Third anchor, adapted from the Freelancer.com brief "Travel-Themed T-Shirt Design", which asked for "layered vector files (AI or EPS) plus high-resolution PNGs with transparent backgrounds", to "keep text editable", and for artwork "sized and pre-flighted for screen print or DTG". None of the posts names a client, so the label is laundered to the coined fictional Cordwain Overland. Two things are held out of scope deliberately: the Freelancer post's from scratch art creation, which is not connector work, and the earlier version of this slot's inversion into a report only audit whose every finding required measurement the agent cannot perform. The verdict is STRENGTHEN, so the concept and the collateral set are kept: three recovered vector graphics, per graphic spot colour separation sheets, a one colour reduction of each for dark garments, a garment mockup board on licensed apparel shots, a printer spec sheet naming plates, inks, placement and maximum print width, and a square teaser set for the store page. What is deepened is the depth around them: the three graphics arrive in three different states and need three different correct routes, the printer's own submission sheet is a real press PDF that has to be reverse engineered into a record per page run, and the marks have to be judged at the size they actually print rather than at canvas size.
client_one_liner: We lost the layered art for three of our best selling graphics, all we have left is a few flat exports and two printed samples, and the spring drop goes to the printer in three weeks.
client_brief:
Cordwain Overland, spring merch drop

We are a small overland and hiking apparel label in Bend. Tees at thirty four dollars, hoodies at seventy eight, sold through our own store and four independent outfitters. Our graphics are the reason people buy: our customers zoom in on the print detail before they add to cart.

We have a problem. Our old designer worked off site and we never got the layered files. When he stopped answering, we were left with whatever was sitting in our shared folder: three flat exports of our three best selling graphics, saved at whatever size was to hand at the time, and two printed samples we photographed on the bench so we could remember what the inks actually looked like. That is everything.

The spring drop reprints all three, on light and on dark garments, and it goes to our printer in three weeks. He needs each graphic as artwork he can actually burn screens from, one sheet per graphic showing him each ink as its own plate, and he needs a one ink version of each for the dark garments, because he charges per screen and three plates on a hoodie prices us out of our own line.

We also need something to show him and something to show our customers. For the printer, our drop submitted on his own form, one page per graphic per garment colour, with the ink names he stocks, the placement and the widest we want each one printed. His blank form is attached, along with his ink list. For the store page, a board showing each graphic on the actual garment, and a set of square teasers.

A note on how it should feel. Thirty four dollar tees, buyers twenty four to forty who care about how a print is made. Two or three tight inks with a bit of texture reads as quality to them. A muddy six colour job reads as a bargain bin and would misprice the whole line.

Tell us what you found, what you had to rebuild and anything our printer should know.
price_band_and_audience: Mid tier outdoor apparel, tees at thirty four dollars and hoodies at seventy eight, buyers twenty four to forty who screenshot the print detail before they buy and who can tell a discharge print from a thick plastisol slab. The band is load-bearing in a way that shows in the plates themselves. At this price a tight two or three ink separation with visible texture and honest registration reads as craft, and the customer pays for it. Ship the same three graphics as a six or seven colour simulated process job and the print reads heavy and cheap on the garment, the printer's per screen charge doubles, and a thirty four dollar tee is suddenly priced like a forty five dollar one that looks worse. Push the other way into a single thin one ink line on every garment and the line stops being a graphics led brand at all, which is the only reason these customers buy. The one colour reduction is therefore a deliberate reduction for dark garments and cost, not a default, and treating it as the master is as wrong as shipping seven plates. A real posted job of this shape runs 900 to 2,400 dollars fixed.

brand_identity.tagline: Made for the long way round
brand_identity.sector: Mid tier overland and hiking apparel label selling graphic tees and hoodies through its own store and four independent outfitters
brand_identity.founded_place_size: Founded 2016 in Bend, Oregon; a small independent label, a handful of people, direct to consumer plus four stockists
brand_identity.about: Cordwain Overland makes graphic apparel for people who drive the back roads and walk the ridgelines. Our graphics are the reason people buy: customers zoom in on the print detail before they add to cart. Every drop is a small set of designs printed with care on garments meant to be worn hard.
brand_identity.audience: Buyers aged twenty four to forty who care how a print is made, can tell a discharge print from a thick plastisol slab, and screenshot the print detail before they buy
brand_identity.price_positioning: Tees at thirty four dollars, hoodies at seventy eight. Mid tier: a clear step above a bargain blank, priced on print quality rather than logo. Two or three tight inks with a bit of texture read as the craft they pay for.
brand_identity.typography: A sturdy condensed sans for badge and display work, paired with a plain workhorse sans for spec sheets and store copy. Type inside the graphics is treated as drawn lettering, outlined to print. The feel is field manual, not fashion label.
brand_identity.voice: Direct, plainspoken and a little dry; we talk about how a thing is made, not how it will change your life. Example line the brand would write: "Three tight inks, printed to last the season."
brand_identity.brand_assets_status: The brand sheet is two pages of internal notes: the palette in words, the placement rules we have always used, our maximum print widths for chest and full back, and a paragraph on what we mean by a tight print. Our old designer worked off site and we never got the layered files; for three of our best selling graphics all that survives is a few flat web exports and two printed samples we photographed on the bench.
brand_identity.values: The print is the product. We would rather run two or three honest inks with real texture than a muddy multi colour job, and we never price the line out of its own customers.

assets_supplied.name: cordwain_flat_exports/ (3 PNGs: ridgeline_back.png 2400px, compass_chest.png 1800px, overland_badge.png 600px)
assets_supplied.kind: Flat web exports of the three graphics, all on white, saved by the previous designer at whatever size was to hand.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The three graphics as we last exported them. Ridgeline is the full back one, compass is the chest print, badge is the one on the hoodies."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The compass export was round-tripped through JPEG at some point before it was saved back out, so its ink fields carry compression mottling that is completely invisible on white at web scale but that a trace resolves into dozens of near identical fills instead of two clean plates, and the trace tool takes no options at all so there is no threshold or colour count to tune it with. The badge export is only 600 pixels, far below anything a hoodie chest print can be built from, and all three sit on an opaque white ground that the trace will carry through as a full canvas rectangle underneath the artwork.

assets_supplied.name: cordwain_sample_photos/ (2 JPEGs, 4000 x 3000)
assets_supplied.kind: Photographs of two printed samples taken on the studio bench in daylight: a light tee carrying the compass print, and a dark hoodie carrying the overland badge.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The printed samples. These are the only record of what the inks actually looked like once they were on fabric."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The badge on the hoodie is a compound lockup, a type ring set around an enclosed centre with a hairline rule between them, so background removal returns a solid opaque disc with the enclosed centre still filled by the garment, and a prompt naming the garment or the sample pulls the selection to the hoodie rather than to the ink. On the tee, the compass lettering is disjoint, so subject detection keeps only a couple of letters and drops the rest while reporting success.

assets_supplied.name: cordwain_printer_submission.pdf
assets_supplied.kind: The printer's blank artwork submission sheet as a press PDF, one page: an artwork window, a graphic name and garment colour block, an ink name list, and a placement and maximum print width footer.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "His form. He will not accept artwork any other way, and he wants one page per graphic per garment colour."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The ink name list is a fixed measure frame that does not spill: a stocked ink name longer than the measure simply stops rendering at the trim edge, silently, so the printer receives a truncated ink name that still looks like a complete one, and the merge reports success throughout. What the printed form shows as four separate blocks is also not necessarily what the conversion exposes as separate frames.

assets_supplied.name: cordwain_printer_inkbook.txt
assets_supplied.kind: The printer's stocked ink list: ink names, whether each is available as discharge or plastisol, and a garment colour compatibility column.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "What he actually keeps on the shelf. He will substitute if we ask for something he does not stock, and we would rather he did not."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Several of the stocked names run long enough to matter downstream, and the compatibility column, which only pays off if it is cross read against garment colour rather than read down, shows that two of the hues recovered from the samples have no discharge equivalent on dark garments at all, which is precisely where the one ink reduction is needed.

assets_supplied.name: cordwain_brand_sheet.md
assets_supplied.kind: Two pages of internal notes: the palette described in words, the placement rules the label has always used, the maximum print widths for chest and full back, and a paragraph on what they mean by a tight print.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "How we brief the printer, written down for once."

assets_supplied.name: cordwain_store_grabs/ (4 PNGs)
assets_supplied.kind: Screengrabs of the current store product pages, supplied so the teasers sit correctly beside existing tiles.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "How the store page looks now. The teasers have to live next to these."

acceptance_bar: Each of the three graphics is delivered as placeable, scalable vector geometry: a real viewBox present, no opaque full canvas rectangle riding underneath it, and a transparent ground so it composites on any garment colour.

Each graphic still reads as the same graphic at the size it actually prints, on the garment colour it actually prints on. A mark whose counters or hairlines close up at chest print size on dark fabric fails even if it is perfect at canvas size.
Each separation sheet shows each ink as its own plate, and a plate is a plate: a flat single ink field, not a posterised approximation carrying dozens of near identical fills.
No graphic exceeds three plates, and every ink named is one the printer actually stocks, checked against the garment colour it is going on rather than in isolation.
Each graphic has a one ink reduction that still reads as that graphic rather than as a silhouette of it, and the reduction is presented as a reduction for dark garments and cost, not as the master.
No delivered raster exceeds the pixel dimensions of the source it derives from, and no returned tradeoff record in the run carries an upscale entry.
The mockup board shows each graphic at true relative size on a real garment photograph, and the three garment shots read as one lookbook rather than as three purchases.
The printer submission run is one press ready file, one page per graphic per garment colour, in the order the run was specified, with the artwork window carrying that row's own artwork.
No ink name, graphic name or print width on any submission page is cut off at the trim edge.
The separation sheets, the mockup board and the store teasers carry one type system, with the note naming per role the family, its foundry or type designer and the actual numeric weight used.
The store teasers and the separation sheets arrive as a working file the label can edit, with the marks present as real vector shapes and the words as text they can retype.

The note records what was recovered from what, which graphic had to be rebuilt by a different route and why, every ink substitution and why, and everything the printer needs to know that is not on his own form.

adobe_surfaces.surface: Photoshop and Lightroom imaging, including image_vectorize which is counted HERE and not as an Illustrator surface
adobe_surfaces.tools: asset_initialize_file_upload / asset_finalize_file_upload, asset_inline_preview, image_select_by_prompt (returnBbox), image_select_subject, image_invert_selection, image_fill_area, image_apply_adjustments (masked), image_apply_monochromatic_tint, image_apply_halftone (masked), image_add_grain, image_crop_to_bounds, image_crop_and_resize, image_remove_background, image_vectorize
adobe_surfaces.role: The whole recovery and separation half of the commission. It triages three graphics that arrive in three different states, traces the two exports that can be traced as they stand, recovers the third at ink level off a photographed garment where naming the substrate takes the hoodie instead of the ink and background removal cannot punch an enclosed centre, isolates each ink field and flattens it so a plate is genuinely one ink, builds each one colour reduction, and performs the vector hygiene the trace tool does not do for itself.

adobe_surfaces.surface: Adobe Stock and Adobe Boards, counted as ONE surface
adobe_surfaces.tools: asset_search (entityScope StockAsset, SHORT generic queries, contentType filter, never orientation), asset_license_and_download_stock, boards_create_new_board, boards_add_items_to_board
adobe_surfaces.role: The blank garment photography the mockup board sits on, which the label does not have and cannot shoot in three weeks. Candidates are chosen for whether their light and fabric can be brought to one lookbook target, at genuine camera scale because nothing downstream may enlarge, with generative tech excluded. The Boards half persists the shareable sign off set the printer and the store manager both work from, inside the per call placement cap, with a partial success read as partial and vector understood to be unacceptable there.

adobe_surfaces.tools: font_recommend (once per typographic role), font_styles, find_fonts, get_fontkit_embed_url
adobe_surfaces.role: The type system for the separation sheets, the spec sheet and the store teasers. It is deliberately not the type inside the graphics: the lettering in the marks is recovered as outlined vector geometry, which is what the printer needs and what the anchor brief asks for. The recommender refuses to pair by design, so the pairing is the agent's own art direction against a thirty four dollar outdoor band; numeric weights are non standard per family and cannot be inferred from a style name, and one unresolvable name destroys the whole kit.

adobe_surfaces.surface: Adobe Express, HTML authoring to a native editable document
adobe_surfaces.tools: get_account_type, create_visual_design_express_skill, html_export_readiness_skill, asset_initialize_file_upload / asset_finalize_file_upload with media_type text/html, export_html_to_express({url}), asset_search (CCAsset), asset_get_presigned_urls, asset_inline_preview
adobe_surfaces.role: The separation sheets, the mockup board and the square store teasers as one native editable document at mixed canvas sizes. This is also the only lawful way to put a graphic onto a garment photograph here, because that is a layout act rather than an image edit: the garment photograph goes in as embedded image data and the mark goes on top as inline vector inside an explicitly sized top left anchored wrapper, staying editable rather than being flattened into the photo.

adobe_surfaces.tools: convert_pdf_to_indd, export_idml, generate_indd_mapping_prompt (including its validator mode), prepare_indd_merge_template, document_merge_data_layout, document_render_layout
adobe_surfaces.role: The printer submission run on the printer's own form, one page per graphic per garment colour, which is a genuine record per page job and the one deliverable that cannot be authored anywhere else because the form belongs to the printer. The blank press PDF is reverse engineered into a live merge template, offsets are computed from the document's true story text rather than from its summary, the per row artwork is bound through the image column in the exact shape the merge requires, and the run is delivered as one press file plus proofs rendered at real resolution.

trajectory.action: Confirm the account tier, pull the authoring playbook, and settle which deliverable lands on which surface, including where a graphic may lawfully be placed onto a garment photograph.
trajectory.judgement: Putting a mark on a garment shot is a layout act on the authoring surface, not an image edit, because compositing one photograph into another is not available here. Getting that wrong at the planning stage sends the whole mockup deliverable down a route that does not exist.
trajectory.produces: A written plan naming surface per deliverable and the confirmed account tier that gates the export at the end.

trajectory.action: Upload every supplied asset through initialize, PUT and finalize, holding each returned presigned URL against its role.
trajectory.judgement: Ordinary handover discipline: three exports, two samples, a press PDF, an ink list and a brand sheet all have to stay individually addressable through forty artefacts of work.
trajectory.produces: A manifest of presigned URLs keyed by role.

trajectory.action: Look at all five raster inputs and triage them: which export is large enough to carry the print it is for, which graphic survives only on a photographed garment, and what each mark is actually made of in terms of ink count and enclosed shapes.
trajectory.judgement: The three graphics look like three of the same thing and are not. The badge export is a sixth the size of the back print export, and no crop or resize can add detail that was never saved, so at least one of the three has to be recovered from a photograph rather than from a file.
trajectory.produces: A per graphic triage note naming the recovery route for each and the reason.

trajectory.action: Trace the two exports that are large enough to trace, then perform the hygiene the trace does not do: inject a viewBox and remove the opaque full canvas ground path from each result.
trajectory.judgement: A flat export is exactly the input a trace expects, so this is the correct first move for both. The hygiene is not optional: without a viewBox the geometry will not scale, and the ground path shows as a white box the moment the mark lands on a garment colour.
trajectory.produces: Traced geometry for the two exports, each with a viewBox present and the ground path removed.

trajectory.action: Recover the third graphic off the photographed hoodie: select the ink by its own visual properties rather than by the garment it sits on, correct the polarity, crop to the selection's own returned bounds, trace, and apply the same hygiene.
trajectory.judgement: Three decisions the tools do not make: how to word the selection so it takes the ink and not the fabric, which polarity to trace so the result is a positive mark rather than a knocked out box, and that background removal is the wrong instrument entirely on a lockup with an enclosed centre because it returns a solid disc.
trajectory.produces: Master geometry for the badge, recovered at ink level from a photograph rather than from a file.

trajectory.action: Derive each graphic's plate structure: isolate each ink field, flatten it to a single ink, and trace each plate on its own, checking the count against what the band can carry.
trajectory.judgement: A separation is a set of plates, not a posterised picture of the artwork. The plate count is a pricing decision as much as a craft one, because the printer charges per screen and three plates on a hoodie prices the line out of itself.
trajectory.produces: Per graphic plate sets, each plate a flat single ink field, with the plate count recorded per graphic.

trajectory.action: Build the one ink reduction of each graphic for dark garments, deciding per graphic what carries the mark when only one ink is left.
trajectory.judgement: A reduction is a redraw decision, not a threshold. Whether the ridgeline reads through its silhouette or through its horizon lines, and whether the badge survives without its inner rule, are judgements a tool cannot make and a customer at this band will notice immediately.
trajectory.produces: Three one ink reductions, each still legible as its own graphic.

trajectory.action: Search short generic queries for blank garment photography, filtered to photography, reading true full resolution dimensions and excluding generative tech, then license and download immediately at full resolution.
trajectory.judgement: Long descriptive queries return nothing and the orientation filter always returns zero, so neither is used. The choice is which shots' fabric and light can be brought to one lookbook target together, not which thumbnail is nicest.
trajectory.produces: Licensed garment photography at camera scale with asset id, contributor and licence state recorded.

trajectory.action: Bring the licensed garment shots to one lookbook target with a call each, recording the parameters applied.
trajectory.judgement: Three shots by three contributors will not take one identical parameter set. The target is a set: one white point, one fabric warmth, one shadow character, so the board reads as a lookbook rather than as three purchases.
trajectory.produces: A graded garment set at source scale with a per frame parameter log.

trajectory.action: Ask for recommendations once per typographic role, pull the family style inventories for the real numeric weights, launder every name into canonical form, and build one kit.
trajectory.judgement: The pairing is the agent's own art direction, judged against a thirty four dollar outdoor band and a buyer who reads print craft. The weight cannot be inferred from a style name, a display cut is reached by its own slug, and one unresolvable name destroys the entire kit.
trajectory.produces: A one kit type system with family, foundry or designer and actual numeric weight recorded per role.

trajectory.action: Author one self contained document carrying the three separation sheets, the mockup board and the square teasers at their own canvas sizes: marks as inline vector inside explicitly sized top left anchored wrappers, garment photographs embedded as image data, family and weight declared on every text element, then upload the file and hold the returned URL.
trajectory.judgement: An anchored auto sized wrapper throws its contents off the artboard, a photograph left as a reference is not a photograph, and a global canvas override collapses a mixed size set. The design work is placing each mark on each garment at its true relative print size rather than at whatever size fills the panel.
trajectory.produces: One export ready source document carrying every authored canvas, retained as the durable deliverable.

trajectory.action: Run the readiness check, export by URL, then verify through both channels: resolve the document's rendition and look at canvas one, and parse the returned per canvas markup for the rest.
trajectory.judgement: Every drop this importer performs returns success with no warning, and the rendition only ever shows the first artboard. Marks that arrive as many loose shapes are editable but not necessarily usable, and that distinction belongs in the handover.
trajectory.produces: A native editable document, an inspected first canvas, and a per canvas markup audit for the remainder.

trajectory.action: Convert the printer's blank submission sheet, export the document structure, and inspect what the conversion actually exposes: how many text frames, what each holds, and whether the artwork window survives as a linkable frame.
trajectory.judgement: The printed form shows four separate blocks; that is not evidence about the document. Nothing can be promised about which field lands where until this has been looked at.
trajectory.produces: A true frame inventory for the converted submission sheet.

trajectory.action: Reconstruct the sheet's true story text from the exported document's own story runs, compute every offset from that string, build and validate the mapping, prepare the merge template, then export the structure again and confirm every placeholder is genuinely present.
trajectory.judgement: The structure summary is not the text, and a mapping built from the summary can validate and prepare cleanly while landing only some of its fields. The only proof is the document itself.
trajectory.produces: A merge template whose placeholders are confirmed present by inspection rather than by a success message.

trajectory.action: Author the submission data, one row per graphic per garment colour, with ink names taken from the printer's stocked list checked against each row's garment colour, the artwork column in the exact shape the merge binds images from, then merge to one press file in run order and render proofs at real resolution.
trajectory.judgement: The ink names are a substitution decision, not a transcription: two recovered hues have no discharge equivalent on dark garments, which only shows by cross reading the compatibility column against the garment colour. The image column has to be in the form the merge reads or every page silently takes no artwork, and the merge tool ignores the resolution asked of it, so proofs have to be rendered separately.
trajectory.produces: One press ready submission file, one page per graphic per garment colour, plus proofs at real resolution.

trajectory.action: Create the sign off board and add the graded garment set, the mockup canvases and the reductions within the per call placement cap, re-sending only the entries the response names as failed.
trajectory.judgement: A partial success is reported as a success, so the failed list is the only thing worth reading, and vector artwork is not boardable so the marks go into the note instead.
trajectory.produces: A persistent shareable board for the printer and the store manager with nothing silently dropped.

trajectory.action: Write the printer spec content and the note: plate list and ink per graphic, placement and maximum print width, what was recovered from what, which graphic had to be rebuilt by a different route and why, every ink substitution and why, and what the printer needs to know that is not on his own form.
trajectory.judgement: The note is the only place the archaeology survives. It has to be specific enough that the next reprint does not repeat it, and honest enough to name anything that could not be delivered.
trajectory.produces: A printer facing spec sheet and a written handover note.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether each flat export is actually flat at pixel level. The compass export was round-tripped through JPEG at some point before it was saved back out, so its two ink fields carry compression mottling that is completely invisible on white at web scale and completely invisible in a preview, and the trace resolves it into dozens of near identical fills instead of two clean plates. The trace tool takes no options at all, no colour count, no threshold, no path simplification, so there is no parameter that would have prevented it and no reading of the file that would have predicted it. The other export traces cleanly on exactly the same call.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering does not dodge it, because tracing the export is the first and correct thing to do with a file the client calls a flat export, and there is nothing to trace against beforehand. Doing it right the first time would mean flattening the ink fields of every export before tracing any of them, which is work with no reason on a genuinely flat file and which would additionally destroy the three ink structure of the back print graphic if done blind. Nothing states it: the brief says only that the exports were saved at whatever size was to hand. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is a different chain, selecting each ink field by its own visual properties, inverting and filling it to a single flat ink, and only then tracing.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Take the affected graphic off the direct trace route, isolate each of its ink fields and flatten each to a single ink in the raster before tracing, then re-apply the hygiene to the new result and re-derive its plates and its one ink reduction from the rebuilt master rather than from the first trace.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A separation sheet the printer cannot burn screens from: dozens of near identical fills presented as two plates, which either comes back as a rejected submission or, worse, gets separated by the printer's own operator into something nobody at the label chose.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether the recovered marks still hold at the size they actually print, on the ground they actually print on. All three traces look correct at canvas size on white. At a three and a half inch chest print on a dark hoodie, the badge's hairline rule between its type ring and its enclosed centre and the counters inside its smallest letters close up into solid ink, and the compass graphic's finest bearing lines thicken until the rose reads as a blob. Which strokes close is a property of what the trace produced from that particular input, and it is only visible once the mark is placed at true relative size on a real garment photograph and rendered.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: No ordering avoids it, because the mark has to exist and be placed before it can be judged at reproduction size, and the authoring surface is the only place a mark can be put on a garment at true relative scale. Doing it right the first time presumes knowing in advance which strokes a trace will render thin enough to close, which no response reports. Nothing states it: the brief asks for a tight print and gives maximum print widths, which is the client's own art direction and their standing spec, not a warning that a recovered stroke will close. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is upstream and different, a thickened or removed rule and a redrawn counter treatment in the raster prep before re-tracing, or a decision that the affected element belongs only in the light garment version.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Go back into the raster prep for the affected marks, adjust the elements that close so the trace produces geometry that survives at print size, re-trace, re-apply hygiene, re-derive the affected plates and reductions, then re-author and re-export the mockup and separation canvases and judge them again at true relative size rather than at canvas size.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A drop that prints as a blob on the exact detail these customers zoom in on before they buy, on a label whose entire premium over a bargain tee is the quality of the print.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether the submission pages say what they appear to say. The ink name list on the printer's form is a fixed measure frame that does not spill: a stocked ink name longer than the measure simply stops rendering at the trim edge. The merge reports success, the page count is right, the pages are in order, and the truncated name still reads as a complete, plausible ink name, so nothing anywhere flags it. Which rows are affected depends on which stocked names the substitution decision landed on and which garment colour each row is for, so it cannot be predicted from either the form or the ink list alone.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering does not dodge it: the frame measure is a property of the supplied press PDF and the names are a property of the printer's stocked list, and the two only meet on the merged page. There is no parameter that reflows or shrinks the text, and nothing in any response reports an overset. Nothing states it: the client says only that the printer will not accept artwork any other way. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is a different mapping, moving the stocked ink name into the wider notes frame and putting the printer's short code into the constrained one, which means recomputing offsets against the true story text and preparing the template again rather than merging the same template again.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Re-map the affected field to a frame that can carry it, recompute every offset against the reconstructed story text, re-prepare the template, confirm the placeholders again by inspection, re-merge the whole run and read every page at trim to its final character rather than reading the first page and the page count.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A submission the printer accepts and works from in which the ink named on some pages is not the ink the label chose, discovered on press, on a drop with three weeks of lead time and no second run.

deliverables.name: Cordwain master graphics, three recovered marks
deliverables.spec: All three graphics as placeable, scalable vector geometry with a real viewBox present, no opaque full canvas rectangle underneath and a transparent ground, recovered by whichever route each one's surviving material actually allows, and each holding together at the size it genuinely prints on the garment colour it prints on. Delivered with each graphic's per ink plate set, each plate a flat single ink field rather than a posterised approximation, and a one ink reduction of each for dark garments that still reads as that graphic. This is one system of three marks with one hygiene standard, not one mark at several sizes.

deliverables.name: Cordwain garment lookbook rasters
deliverables.spec: The licensed blank garment photography brought to one lookbook target, one white point, one fabric warmth and one shadow character, so that three shots from three contributors read as one shoot behind the store page. Delivered at camera scale with a per frame parameter log and with the licence state and contributor recorded per frame. Nothing generative tech, nothing enlarged.

deliverables.name: Separation sheets, mockup board and store teasers, as one editable document plus its source
deliverables.spec: One native editable document carrying the three separation sheets, the mockup board and the square store teasers, each root keeping its own canvas size, with the marks present as real vector shapes rather than pictures of shapes, the garment photographs carried as embedded image data, each mark shown at true relative print size on the garment, and one licensed type system across every canvas. Delivered with the self contained source it was authored from, which is the durable half.

deliverables.name: Printer submission run on the printer's own form
deliverables.spec: One press ready file, one page per graphic per garment colour in the order the run was specified, each page carrying that row's graphic name, garment colour, stocked ink names, placement and maximum print width, with the artwork window carrying that row's own artwork rather than one image repeated across the run, and with no field cut off at the trim edge. Paired with proof rasters rendered at real resolution for sign off rather than at the merge default.

deliverables.name: Printer spec sheet, recovery note and sign off board
deliverables.spec: A printer facing spec naming per graphic the plate list, the stocked ink per plate checked against garment colour, the placement and the maximum print width. A note recording what was recovered from what, which graphic had to be rebuilt by a different route and why, every ink substitution and the compatibility reason for it, the type system by role with family, foundry or designer and actual numeric weight, and anything the printer needs to know that his own form does not ask for. Paired with a persistent shareable sign off board for the printer and the store manager with nothing silently dropped.

decision_gates: Which deliverables are raster and vector recovery work, which need an authored fixed canvas document, and which need a record per page run on a form the client does not own.
That placing a graphic onto a garment photograph is a layout act on the authoring surface rather than an image edit, because compositing one photograph into another is not available here.
Recovery route per graphic: trace the export as it stands, flatten the ink fields first, or abandon the export entirely and recover the mark at ink level off a photographed garment.

Selection wording on the photographed sample: naming the garment or the sample takes the fabric, naming the ink's own visual properties takes the mark, and background removal is the wrong instrument on a lockup with an enclosed centre.
How many plates each graphic gets, which is simultaneously a craft judgement and a pricing judgement because the printer charges per screen.
What carries each graphic when only one ink is left, which is a redraw decision rather than a threshold.
Which stocked inks to name per row, cross read against garment colour rather than read down the list, and how to say so when two recovered hues have no discharge equivalent on dark garments.
Which licensed garment shots can be brought to one lookbook target together, judged on their fabric and light rather than on the thumbnail.

The type pairing for the sheets and teasers, which the recommender refuses to make, judged against a thirty four dollar outdoor band and a buyer who reads print craft, plus the real numeric weight per family.
At what size each mark is shown on the garment, since the print width is the client's spec and filling the panel is the correct looking wrong answer.
Which fields the converted submission sheet can actually carry, given that the printed form is not evidence about the document's structure.
why_not_vlm: Paste the brief and the assets into a frontier image model and it returns three attractive outdoor t-shirt graphics. IDENTITY: these are this label's three best selling graphics, the ones its customers already own and recognise, and a regenerated mountain and compass is a different label's artwork; the whole commission exists because the layered files were lost, so recovery is the job and reinvention is the failure. SPEC: a screen printer needs one plate per ink as a flat single ink field, a plate count the pricing can carry, ink names from his own stocked list checked against garment colour, and a submission on his own form at one page per graphic per garment colour, none of which a generated picture is or can be checked to be. EDITABILITY: the anchor briefs ask explicitly for layered vector with spot colour information and for artwork sized and pre-flighted for screen print, and a flat raster satisfies none of it. And the middle of this engagement is verification against material reality: did this export trace into two plates or into dozens of fills, does this hairline survive at three and a half inches on a hoodie, does this ink name fit the frame it lands in.
doability_proof: Every link is verified live in CONNECTOR_CAPABILITIES_v3 (2026-09-10, auth account), five surfaces honestly counted with image_vectorize counted as a Photoshop family tool rather than an Illustrator surface, no banned capability and no dead surface. IMAGING: select_by_prompt with returnBbox, select_subject, invert_selection, fill_area, apply_adjustments masked, monochromatic_tint, halftone masked, add_grain, crop_to_bounds, crop_and_resize with its tradeoffs, remove_background and vectorize are all verified headless across 27 live calls, including the exact recovery chain used here (select the ink, invert, crop to the returned bounds, trace) which produced a three path outline of a printed mark with its strokes intact off a photographed surface. The checkpoints rest on documented findings rather than assumptions: vectorize TAKES NO OPTIONS AT ALL so all tuning must happen in the raster prep and a colour plate in yields dozens of near identical fills out; the substrate versus ink prompt asymmetry is verified (naming the object returned the card, naming the ink's colour and medium returned the strokes); remove_background returns a SOLID OPAQUE DISC on an enclosed ring and keeps only a couple of letters of a disjoint wordmark; the trace always emits an opaque full canvas path zero and no viewBox; and a traced mark lands in Express as many loose path shapes, which is why editability and usability are separated in the acceptance bar. EXPRESS: mixed canvas sizes in one export are verified, inline SVG becomes native editable vector, an inline SVG must sit in a wrapper with explicit left, top, width and height or its contents run off the canvas, photographs must be embedded as image data because every external reference resolved to a placeholder at full success, canvasWidth and canvasHeight are never passed as tool params, transport is pinned through asset upload with media_type text/html, and verification is split between the rendition (page one only) and the returned per canvas markup. This is also the lawful route for putting a mark on a garment, since photo compositing is unavailable and this is layout. STOCK AND BOARDS: short generic queries only, orientation never passed because it always returns zero, license returned a genuine 7360x4912 JPEG, the download link expires in one hour, and boards persist with a hard cap of twelve placements per call and 201 meaning partial. FONTS: recommend once per role, styles for the non standard numeric weights, find_fonts to launder names because one bad name kills the whole kit, and the CSS uses the returned slug. INDESIGN: convert_pdf_to_indd, export_idml, generate_indd_mapping_prompt with its validator mode, prepare_indd_merge_template, document_merge_data_layout and document_render_layout are all verified fully headless and synchronous; one record per page is confirmed for PDF output; frame granularity from a PDF is verified as not under the author's control; per row image binding requires the @ prefixed CSV header with bare filenames and matching additionalImageFiles keys; and real resolution requires document_render_layout because outputSpecs.resolution is silently ignored. AVOIDED: no video or audio, no vector render or vector merge, no variable QR, no bleed gate, no pdfPreset, no fill_text, no animate_design, no replace_image, no text to image, no generative fill, no compositing, no OCR, no upscaling, no batch above 20.
